source_reviews.independent_solution: Gravity acts toward the ground in the lesson's terrestrial setting. Loss of support lets an initially resting object fall, and gravity-induced loading can deform its support through the object's contact action. A supported object can remain at rest while still experiencing gravity, because a distinct support force balances its weight. Supported rest neither switches gravity off nor reverses it. Balanced forces alone do not instantaneously remove an existing velocity. This solution was saved in source-blind.md before reading the learner view or any key.

source_reviews.independent_solution: An elastically deformed body tends to recover its original shape or size and exerts an elastic force on a body in contact with it. The bent horizontal support pushes upward in the particular example; a stretched spring or string acts at its attachment, and a horizontally stretched spring can pull horizontally. Thus deformation and contact define the interaction, mere contact is insufficient, and vertically upward is not universal. This independent definition and direction counterexample were saved in source-blind.md before reading the learner view or any key.

Gravity remains toward the ground during supported rest; the upward support force is a different force. The author's attribution of the upward support action to gravity is precisely the mistaken procedure that yields D.

mathematics.independent_solution: The independently saved complete true set is A and D. An elastically deformed body exerts an elastic force on a body in contact with it; direction depends on the actual deformation/contact geometry. A horizontally stretched spring refutes C's universal upward claim. Non-contact action in B and contact without elastic deformation in E do not define elastic force. The author's key, all five truth labels, derivations, and concrete misconceptions agree after comparison.

option_checks.evidence: A states deformation as the origin and contact as the relationship through which the deformed body acts. This correctly abstracts the bent board acting on its supported object. The author's definition derivation agrees and correctly uses null misconception.

Elastic action on a spring attachment or a supported body requires contact. Substituting non-contact for contact converts the interaction into a different category. The author's proposed mistaken extension from deformation to remote action genuinely yields B and is false here.

A horizontal stretched spring pulls an attached object horizontally, providing a concrete counterexample to vertically upward in every contact situation. The author's overgeneralization from the horizontal-board example is the actual false procedure in C.

Changing contact and deformation geometry can change the elastic-force direction: an upward board support and a horizontal spring force are both consistent. The author's direction-by-configuration derivation agrees; the option does not assert a universal upward force.

Mere touching does not suffice to establish a restoring elastic force in the absence of elastic deformation. The author's misconception correctly removes the causal deformation requirement and treats contact alone as sufficient, exactly as E states.
